terra-nova-cardiff-harbour-1910.head: In June 1910, Captain Scott's ship, the Terra Nova, left the Welsh port of Cardiff for Antarctica.
terra-nova-cardiff-harbour-1910.body: Robert Falcon Scott's second Antarctic expedition is known as the Terra Nova Expedition, after its ship. The ship left London on the first of June 1910, but its final departure from Britain was from Cardiff, in Wales, on the fifteenth of June. Cardiff was then one of the busiest coal ports in the world. Welsh businesses gave the expedition coal, money and supplies, and the people of the city gave the crew a warm farewell. Historians know about the departure from newspapers, diaries and photographs. The expedition aimed to reach the South Pole and to carry out a large programme of scientific research. Even so, it was not well funded. Scott had to raise money from businesses, schools and the public, and the government gave only part of the cost. When the ship sailed out of Cardiff, crowds cheered from the docks. Few could imagine how long the men would be away.

old-wooden-whaling-ship-oak-bow.head: The Terra Nova was an old wooden whaling and sealing ship, built in Dundee in 1884.
old-wooden-whaling-ship-oak-bow.body: The Terra Nova was not a new ship. She had been built in Dundee, in Scotland, in 1884, for the whaling and sealing trade in the Arctic. Her strong wooden hull was designed to push through ice. Scott bought her for the expedition because she was tough and available. She was refitted to carry men, scientific equipment, animals and supplies. Historians note that the ship was cramped and leaked badly, and the crew had to pump water out regularly. She was powered by both sails and a coal-fired steam engine. Even so, she proved her strength many times in heavy seas and thick ice. Sailors described her as a hard but faithful ship. After the expedition, she returned to work in the sealing trade off Newfoundland for many years. She finally sank off the coast of Greenland in 1943. Her figurehead is kept today in the National Museum of Wales in Cardiff.

crowded-ship-deck-crates-hay-coal.head: The deck of the Terra Nova was crowded with crates, coal, fodder and supplies for two years.
crowded-ship-deck-crates-hay-coal.body: The expedition had to carry everything it needed to live and work in Antarctica for at least two years. The Terra Nova was loaded with food, fuel, tents, sledges, scientific instruments, a prefabricated hut, clothing and tools. On deck, there were sacks of coal, bales of hay and fodder for animals, and crates of every size. There was even a motor car and three motor sledges, which were new technology at the time. Historians know about the cargo from lists kept by the expedition and from photographs of the crowded deck. The ship sat very low in the water. Even so, every item had been carefully chosen. Running out of something in Antarctica could be dangerous, since there would be no way to obtain more. The men packed and repacked the cargo many times. They later said that every space on board, from the holds to the cabins, was filled with something needed for the voyage.

antarctica-white-coast-distant-mountains.head: In 1910, much of Antarctica had never been seen by any human being.
antarctica-white-coast-distant-mountains.body: Antarctica is the coldest, windiest and highest continent on Earth. It is covered by an enormous sheet of ice, in places more than four kilometres thick. In 1910, explorers had seen only parts of its coast and had travelled a short distance inland. No one had reached the South Pole. Large areas on the maps were blank. Historians note that the early twentieth century is often called the Heroic Age of Antarctic Exploration. Expeditions from Britain, Norway, Germany, Sweden, Japan and other countries explored the continent with sledges, ships and very simple equipment. Scott had already led an expedition there from 1901 to 1904, on the ship Discovery. Even so, much remained unknown. Scientists did not know what lay beneath the ice, how the weather worked or whether the continent was one land mass. Exploring Antarctica was a journey into one of the last great unknown places on the planet.

naval-captain-ship-deck-thoughtful.head: Robert Falcon Scott was a Royal Navy officer who had already led an expedition to Antarctica.
naval-captain-ship-deck-thoughtful.body: Robert Falcon Scott was born in 1868 in Devon, in the south of England. He joined the Royal Navy as a boy and became an officer. In 1901, he was chosen to lead the Discovery expedition to Antarctica, which explored and mapped large areas and carried out important scientific work. During that expedition, he and two companions travelled further south than anyone before them. When he returned, he became famous. Historians describe Scott as a serious, hardworking and sometimes moody man. He could be strict, but he cared deeply for his men and was devoted to science. He wrote well, and his journals are among the most famous in the history of exploration. Even so, historians have debated his leadership. Some have criticised his decisions, while others have defended them, pointing to bad weather and bad luck. In 1910, he was forty-two years old and determined to reach the Pole.

sculptor-woman-studio-london-1910.head: Scott's wife, Kathleen, was a sculptor who had studied art in Paris.
sculptor-woman-studio-london-1910.body: Kathleen Bruce was born in 1878 and grew up in a large family. She studied art in London and then in Paris, where she met the sculptor Auguste Rodin and other artists. She was independent, adventurous and lively. She married Robert Falcon Scott in 1908, and their son, Peter, was born in 1909. Kathleen supported her husband's plans and helped raise money for the expedition. She travelled with him as far as New Zealand before he sailed for Antarctica. Historians know about their relationship from their many letters and from Kathleen's diaries. Even so, she was also a successful artist in her own right. She later made many sculptures of famous people, including a statue of Scott that stands in London. In 1922, she married again, to the politician Edward Hilton Young. Her son Peter later became a famous naturalist. Kathleen's work can still be seen in museums and public spaces across Britain.

scientists-on-ship-deck-instruments.head: The Terra Nova Expedition carried a large team of scientists as well as explorers.
scientists-on-ship-deck-instruments.body: Scott wanted his expedition to be remembered for science as well as for reaching the Pole. The team included geologists, biologists, a physicist, a meteorologist and other specialists. They planned to study rocks, weather, ice, animals, plants and the magnetism of the Earth. The chief scientist was Edward Wilson, a doctor and naturalist. Historians consider the scientific work of the expedition very important. Its members collected thousands of specimens, made detailed weather records and mapped large areas. Their results were published in many volumes over the following decades. Even so, the scientific work is often forgotten in popular stories, which focus on the race to the Pole. Many scientists of the expedition later had long careers. Some, such as the geologist Griffith Taylor and the physicist Charles Wright, became well known in their fields. The expedition helped lay the foundations of Antarctic science, which continues today at research stations across the continent.

young-men-crew-deck-1910-sun.head: Around eight thousand people applied to join Scott's expedition, but only a few dozen were chosen.
young-men-crew-deck-1910-sun.body: When Scott announced his expedition, thousands of people wanted to join. Historians often repeat that around eight thousand applications arrived. Scott chose men with useful skills, good health and the right character for a long and difficult journey. The team included naval officers and sailors, scientists, a doctor, a photographer, a cook and specialists to care for the animals. Some men had been on the Discovery expedition with Scott. Others came from the army, from universities and from other walks of life. Historians know about the members from their diaries, letters and later memoirs, many of which were published. Even so, the expedition reflected the society of its time. Officers and scientists lived separately from the sailors, and the expedition was entirely made up of men. Yet the members came to know each other closely. Many of them formed friendships that lasted for the rest of their lives, and they wrote warmly about one another.

wardroom-supper-swinging-lamps-ship.head: Life on board the Terra Nova was crowded, but the officers and scientists ate together in a small wardroom.
wardroom-supper-swinging-lamps-ship.body: On the Terra Nova, the officers and scientists shared a small mess room called the wardroom. They ate their meals there and spent evenings talking, reading and playing games. Oil lamps swung from the ceiling as the ship rolled. The sailors had their own quarters at the front of the ship. Space was very limited, and men shared small cabins and bunks. Historians know about life on board from diaries, which describe meals, jokes and the friendships that formed during the voyage. Even so, conditions could be uncomfortable. In rough seas, water leaked into cabins, and many men were seasick. Yet the long voyage helped the team get to know one another before they reached Antarctica. Men from different backgrounds learned to work and live together. Many diaries describe the cheerful atmosphere in the wardroom during the first months, with songs, discussions and plans for the work ahead.

sailing-ship-tropical-sea-flying-fish.head: Before reaching the ice, the Terra Nova sailed through the tropics.
sailing-ship-tropical-sea-flying-fish.body: The voyage from Britain to New Zealand took several months. The Terra Nova sailed south through the Atlantic, stopping at Madeira and South Trinidad, an island off the coast of Brazil, and then at Simon's Town in South Africa. In the tropics, the weather was hot, and the men slept on deck to escape the heat below. They saw flying fish, dolphins and sea birds. The scientists collected samples from the sea and studied the animals they saw. Historians know about this part of the voyage from diaries and from Scott's own journal. Even so, the long voyage was hard work. The ship's engine used large amounts of coal, and the sails had to be handled constantly. From South Africa, the ship continued to Melbourne and then to New Zealand, where final preparations were made. For many of the younger men, the voyage was an exciting adventure, full of new sights before the cold of the south.

stokers-shovelling-coal-furnace-glow.head: Officers and scientists on the Terra Nova took turns helping the stokers shovel coal.
stokers-shovelling-coal-furnace-glow.body: The Terra Nova's steam engine needed a steady supply of coal. In the hot engine room, stokers shovelled coal into the furnaces for hours at a time. It was some of the hardest work on the ship. During the voyage, several officers and scientists volunteered to help with the stoking, working shifts alongside the regular crew. Historians note that this helped build a sense of shared effort. Men who would later lead sledge journeys or carry out scientific work learned what physical labour on the ship involved. Diaries describe the heat, the coal dust and the exhaustion. Even so, many volunteers took pride in the work. It was a way of showing they were willing to do anything for the expedition. The ship also used its sails whenever possible to save coal. Coal was precious, because the ship needed enough for the whole journey to Antarctica and back again to New Zealand.

quiet-man-painting-watercolour-deck.head: Edward Wilson, the chief scientist and doctor, was respected and loved by everyone on the expedition.
quiet-man-painting-watercolour-deck.body: Edward Adrian Wilson was born in 1872 in Cheltenham. He trained as a doctor and was also a talented naturalist and artist. He had sailed with Scott on the Discovery expedition and was one of his closest friends. On the Terra Nova Expedition, he led the scientific team. The men called him Uncle Bill. Historians describe him as calm, kind and deeply religious. Many members of the expedition wrote that he was the person they trusted most. He listened to everyone and helped settle disagreements. Wilson painted beautiful watercolours of Antarctic landscapes, birds and animals. Many of these paintings survive and are kept in museums, including in Cheltenham. Even so, he was also a careful scientist. He studied penguins, seals and birds and made important observations. Wilson was one of the five men who reached the South Pole with Scott. His paintings remain among the finest images of Antarctica from that time.

short-red-haired-officer-ship-stores.head: Henry Bowers, a short and energetic officer, was in charge of the expedition's stores.
short-red-haired-officer-ship-stores.body: Henry Robertson Bowers was born in 1883 in Scotland. He served in the Royal Indian Marine, a naval service in India, before joining the expedition. He was short and strongly built, with red hair and a large nose, which earned him the nickname Birdie. He was in charge of the stores, keeping track of every item of food and equipment. Historians describe him as tireless, cheerful and extremely reliable. Early in the voyage, he fell nineteen feet through an open hatch into the hold. He landed on the pig iron ballast but climbed out almost unhurt and went straight back to work. Even so, at first some members doubted whether he was suited for the expedition, since he had no polar experience. He soon proved himself. Scott came to rely on him completely. Bowers was one of the five men who reached the South Pole, and his organisation was essential to the expedition's success.

tall-army-officer-pipe-reading-corner.head: Captain Lawrence Oates, an army cavalry officer, paid a large sum to join the expedition.
tall-army-officer-pipe-reading-corner.body: Lawrence Edward Grace Oates was born in 1880 into a wealthy family. He served as an officer in the Inniskilling Dragoons, a cavalry regiment, and fought in the Boer War in South Africa, where he was wounded in the leg. He joined the expedition to look after the ponies, which were to help pull sledges. He also paid a thousand pounds towards the cost of the expedition, a large sum at the time. The men called him Titus or the Soldier. Historians describe him as quiet, dry-humoured and honest. He did not always agree with Scott, especially about the choice of ponies. Even so, he worked hard to care for the animals and was respected by the men. Oates was one of the five men who reached the South Pole. His courage on the return journey later became famous across Britain. He is remembered with memorials in his home village of Gestingthorpe and elsewhere.

young-man-round-spectacles-ship-rail.head: Apsley Cherry-Garrard, the youngest officer, later wrote a famous book about the expedition.
young-man-round-spectacles-ship-rail.body: Apsley Cherry-Garrard was born in 1886 and studied at Oxford. He was very short-sighted and had little practical experience, but he was eager to join. He paid towards the cost of the expedition and was taken on as an assistant zoologist. The men called him Cherry. Historians describe him as modest, sensitive and loyal. He edited the expedition's newspaper during the winter and took part in several sledge journeys. In 1922, he published a book about the expedition called The Worst Journey in the World. It describes the expedition's experiences with honesty and great feeling. Historians and readers consider it one of the finest books ever written about exploration. Even so, writing it was difficult for him. The memories of the expedition stayed with him for the rest of his life. His book remains widely read today and has been named by some as the greatest travel book ever written.

lyttelton-harbour-green-hills-1910.head: In New Zealand, the Terra Nova took on the ponies and dogs for the expedition.
lyttelton-harbour-green-hills-1910.body: The Terra Nova arrived in New Zealand in October 1910. There, the expedition made its final preparations in the port of Lyttelton, near Christchurch. The ship was unloaded, repaired and repacked. The ponies and dogs, which had been brought from Siberia and Manchuria by the expedition's dog expert Cecil Meares, were loaded on board. Last letters were written and posted home. Historians know about these weeks from diaries and local newspapers. The people of Christchurch welcomed the expedition warmly, and many visited the ship. Kathleen Scott and other wives said goodbye to their husbands. Even so, there was a serious problem. The ship was dangerously overloaded, carrying far more than it had been designed for. The ship finally sailed from Port Chalmers, further south, on the twenty-ninth of November 1910. The green hills of New Zealand would be the last land the men saw before Antarctica.

men-bailing-buckets-lantern-night-ship.head: In December 1910, a severe storm nearly sank the Terra Nova, and the crew bailed water all night.
men-bailing-buckets-lantern-night-ship.body: Soon after leaving New Zealand, the Terra Nova was struck by a violent storm in the Southern Ocean. Huge waves washed over the deck, and the overloaded ship rolled heavily. Some coal and fuel were lost overboard, and two ponies and a dog died. Water poured into the ship, and the pumps became blocked. The engine fires had to be put out. The men formed a chain and bailed water out with buckets, working through the night. According to diaries, some of them sang as they worked to keep their spirits up. Eventually, a passage was cut to clear the pumps. Historians know about the storm from several detailed accounts. Even so, the ship survived. The men's courage and teamwork were praised by everyone. Scott wrote in his journal about the cheerful way the men had worked. The storm showed how dangerous the voyage was, even before reaching the ice.

first-iceberg-grey-sea-ship.head: As the Terra Nova sailed south, the men saw their first icebergs, some of them enormous.
first-iceberg-grey-sea-ship.body: After the storm, the weather improved, and the ship continued south. In December, the men saw their first icebergs. Some were huge, flat-topped blocks of ice that had broken away from the ice shelves of Antarctica. Others had been shaped by wind and waves into towers and arches. Historians note that Antarctic icebergs can be many kilometres long. The men were amazed by their size and beauty. Diaries describe the changing colours of the ice, from white to blue and green. Even so, icebergs were also dangerous. The ship had to steer carefully around them, especially in fog or at night. As the ship moved further south, the sea became colder, and floating ice became more common. The men knew they were approaching the pack ice, a belt of floating ice that surrounds Antarctica. Getting through it would be the next great challenge of the voyage.

ship-in-pack-ice-midnight-sun.head: On Christmas Day 1910, the Terra Nova was stuck in the pack ice under the midnight sun.
ship-in-pack-ice-midnight-sun.body: The Terra Nova entered the pack ice in December 1910. For weeks, the ship pushed slowly through the floating ice, sometimes stopping completely when the ice closed around her. The men spent Christmas Day 1910 stuck in the pack. In the southern summer, the sun did not set, and it shone all through the night. The men decorated the wardroom, ate a special dinner and sang songs. Historians know about this Christmas from several diaries, which describe the strange beauty of the scene. Even so, the delay was worrying. The ship was using precious coal while waiting, and the season for building a base was short. The men took the opportunity to observe seals and penguins on the ice and to collect scientific samples. Finally, at the end of December, the ice loosened, and the ship broke through into open water. Ahead lay the Ross Sea and the coast of Antarctica.

adelie-penguins-listening-ice-ship.head: Curious penguins often approached the ship, and the sailors sang to them.
adelie-penguins-listening-ice-ship.body: While the ship was in the pack ice, many Adélie penguins came to look at it. Adélie penguins are small, black and white penguins with white rings around their eyes. They are curious and not afraid of people. According to the diaries of the expedition, the penguins would walk up to the ship, and the men noticed that they seemed interested in music. Some sailors sang to them, and the penguins appeared to listen before walking away. Historians enjoy these stories, which show the lighter side of life on the expedition. Scientists of the expedition studied the penguins' behaviour and recorded many observations. Even so, life for the penguins was hard. They had to survive harsh weather and predators such as leopard seals. The men found them very entertaining. Many diaries contain funny descriptions of the penguins' habits, comparing them to little men in evening dress, busy and full of their own importance.

mount-erebus-smoking-volcano-sea.head: One of the first sights of Antarctica for the expedition was Mount Erebus, an active volcano.
mount-erebus-smoking-volcano-sea.body: In early January 1911, the Terra Nova reached Ross Island. The men saw Mount Erebus, a volcano more than three thousand seven hundred metres high, with smoke rising from its summit. It is the southernmost active volcano on Earth. It was named in 1841 by the British explorer James Clark Ross, after one of his ships. Members of Ernest Shackleton's expedition had climbed it in 1908. Historians note that Erebus was a famous landmark for Antarctic expeditions. Wilson painted it many times. Even so, the volcano was not dangerous to the expedition. Its activity was gentle, mostly steam and gas. Scientists today still study it, because it has a rare lake of lava inside its crater. For the men of the Terra Nova, the smoking mountain was a striking sight, rising white and grey above the frozen sea. It became a familiar part of their view for the next two years.

ross-island-coast-cape-black-rocks.head: Scott chose a cape on Ross Island as the site for his base and named it Cape Evans.
ross-island-coast-cape-black-rocks.body: Scott searched for a good place to build his base. He chose a small cape of dark volcanic rock and sand on the west coast of Ross Island. He named it Cape Evans, after his second in command, Lieutenant Edward Evans. The cape was sheltered and had easy access to the sea ice, which the men could use as a road towards the south. It was also some distance from the base of the earlier Discovery expedition at Hut Point. Historians know about the choice from Scott's journal and from maps made by the expedition. Even so, the site had a disadvantage. If the sea ice broke up, the route south would be cut off. The men had to be careful about travelling at certain times of year. Yet Cape Evans proved a good choice for a home. The hut built there still stands today, more than a century later.

ponies-pulling-sledges-sea-ice-ship.head: Unloading the Terra Nova at Cape Evans took days of continuous work.
ponies-pulling-sledges-sea-ice-ship.body: As soon as the base site was chosen, the men began unloading the ship. Everything had to be carried across the sea ice from the ship to the shore. Ponies, dogs and men pulled sledges loaded with crates, coal, fodder and equipment. Because the sun did not set, they worked in shifts through the day and night. Historians know about the unloading from diaries, which describe exhausting but cheerful work. Even so, there were accidents. One of the motor sledges fell through the sea ice and sank. It was a serious loss, since the motor sledges were meant to help carry supplies south. The work continued for about a week. By the end, the beach was covered with stores, and the hut was being built. Diaries describe the satisfaction the men felt when the most important supplies were safely on land, ready for the long months ahead.

wooden-hut-construction-cape-snow.head: The hut at Cape Evans was made in Britain and brought to Antarctica in pieces.
wooden-hut-construction-cape-snow.body: The expedition's hut was designed and built in Britain, then taken apart and carried on the ship in numbered pieces. At Cape Evans, the men put it together like a giant puzzle. It was about fifteen metres long and eight metres wide. The walls were made of wooden boards with layers of insulation, including seaweed in quilted sacks, to keep out the cold. Historians know about its construction from plans, photographs and diaries. The carpenter Frank Davies and other men worked quickly, and the hut was finished in about two weeks. Even so, it was not perfect. Some parts leaked, and the men had to make adjustments. Yet it proved warm and solid enough for the winter. A stable for the ponies was built along one side. The hut would be home for twenty-five men for the next year, and for some of them, for two winters.

hut-cape-evans-erebus-behind-sunlight.head: On calm days at Cape Evans, the only sounds were the sea, the birds and the dogs.
hut-cape-evans-erebus-behind-sunlight.body: In the summer, when the weather was fine, Cape Evans could be a peaceful place. The hut stood on the dark beach, with Mount Erebus rising behind it. The sea ice stretched away towards distant mountains. Penguins and seals lived nearby, and skuas, large brown seabirds, flew overhead. On calm days, the men could hear the sea lapping against the ice, the calls of birds and the occasional barking of the dogs. Historians know about these quiet moments from diaries and from Ponting's photographs, which show the base in calm weather. Even so, the weather could change very quickly. Strong winds, called blizzards, could blow for days, filling the air with snow. Yet the men treasured the calm days. Many wrote about the beauty and silence of the landscape, which seemed to them like no other place on Earth. Some said those days were among the happiest of their lives.

scientist-cutting-hole-sea-ice-net.head: The scientists at Cape Evans studied the sea, the weather and the ice in many different ways.
scientist-cutting-hole-sea-ice-net.body: The scientists of the expedition began their work as soon as the hut was built. Biologists cut holes in the sea ice and lowered nets to catch fish and small sea creatures. Geologists studied the rocks of Ross Island and the surrounding mountains. The meteorologist George Simpson set up instruments to record temperature, wind and air pressure. He also sent balloons into the sky to study the upper atmosphere. Historians consider the expedition's weather records especially valuable. They were among the most detailed made in Antarctica at that time and are still used by scientists today. Even so, the work was difficult in the cold. Instruments froze, and handling equipment with gloves was hard. Yet the scientists persevered. Their notebooks were filled with measurements and observations. Many samples collected by the expedition are still kept in museums, including the Natural History Museum in London, and continue to be studied.

photographer-heavy-camera-tripod-ice.head: Herbert Ponting, the expedition's photographer, took some of the most famous pictures of Antarctica ever made.
photographer-heavy-camera-tripod-ice.body: Herbert George Ponting was born in 1870. Before joining the expedition, he had travelled widely in Asia and become famous for his photographs of Japan. He called himself a camera artist. On the expedition, he photographed the landscapes, the animals, the men and their daily life. He also made moving films, among the first ever made in Antarctica. Historians and art experts consider his work outstanding. His photographs of icebergs, the hut and the expedition members are still widely reproduced. Even so, his work was very difficult. Cameras were heavy, glass plates had to be developed in the cold, and fingers could freeze to metal. Ponting worked patiently, often waiting hours for the right light. He stayed for the first winter and returned home in 1912. Later, he gave lectures and made a film about the expedition, called The Great White Silence, which was restored and re-released in 2011.

killer-whales-ice-edge-calm-water.head: Killer whales once tried to tip Ponting off the ice by breaking it from below.
killer-whales-ice-edge-calm-water.body: Killer whales, also called orcas, live in the waters around Antarctica. They are intelligent hunters that feed on fish, seals and penguins. In January 1911, while the ship was being unloaded, Ponting went out onto the sea ice to photograph a group of killer whales. Suddenly, the whales struck the ice from below, breaking it beneath him. Ponting managed to jump from floe to floe and reach safety. Scott described the event in his journal. Historians note that killer whales sometimes use this method to knock seals or penguins into the water. Even so, it is unclear whether they intended to attack Ponting or simply saw a shape on the ice. Scientists today know much more about killer whale behaviour. In Antarctica, some groups have learned to make waves that wash seals off floating ice. The incident was a reminder that the beautiful landscape also held real dangers for the men.

men-sitting-outside-hut-golden-midnight.head: During the Antarctic summer, the men often sat outside late in the evening to watch the light on the ice.
men-sitting-outside-hut-golden-midnight.body: In the southern summer, the sun circled the sky without setting. Late in the evening, it hung low near the horizon, and the light became golden and pink. Icebergs, mountains and snow glowed in warm colours. After a day of work, the men sometimes sat outside the hut on packing cases, smoking pipes, talking and watching the changing light. Historians know about these evenings from diaries and photographs. Many men wrote about the beauty of the scene and the sense of peace it gave them. Even so, they knew that summer would not last. Each day, the sun dipped a little lower. Soon it would begin to set, and then, for four months, it would not rise at all. The men made the most of the long light, working hard and enjoying the quiet evenings. These moments of calm stayed in their memories long after the expedition was over.

ship-disappearing-horizon-ice-evening.head: When the Terra Nova sailed away in February 1911, twenty-five men stayed behind at Cape Evans.
ship-disappearing-horizon-ice-evening.body: After unloading and building the base, the Terra Nova had to leave before the sea froze. She sailed in late January and February 1911, carrying a small party to explore the coast elsewhere and later returning to New Zealand for the winter. At Cape Evans, the shore party of twenty-five men remained. They watched the ship sail away until it disappeared over the horizon. Historians note that from this moment, the men were completely cut off from the rest of the world. There was no radio, and no news could reach them until the ship returned the following summer. Even so, they were well prepared. The hut was stocked with food and fuel, and they had a full programme of work planned. The men settled into their new home with a mixture of excitement and seriousness. Their adventure in the Antarctic had truly begun, on the edge of a vast and silent continent.
